strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored setting: parameter-efficient continual adaptation of generative LLM recommenders under temporal preference drift.
PESO is simple, computationally lightweight, and maintains constant adapter storage, making it practically attractive compared with cumulative-adapter approaches.

The empirical study is broad in surface coverage, including three main Amazon domains, Yelp, another backbone, numerous continual-LoRA baselines, standard training paradigms, regularizer ablations, and user-group analyses.

The paper is generally well organized, clearly motivates why recommendation differs from conventional task-incremental learning, and provides a useful comparison of cumulative versus evolving LoRA designs.
weaknesses: A stated theoretical result is incorrect: Corollary 4 presents softmax-KL as equal to one-half of a weighted variance up to an additive constant, whereas Proposition 3 establishes only a local second-order approximation with a nonconstant higher-order remainder. Thus, the exact interpretation subsequently used to motivate PESO is unsupported.

The softmax-KL penalty over raw LoRA coordinates is insufficiently justified. It has a constant-shift null direction within every module even though such shifts can substantially change the LoRA update, and it is sensitive to the non-identifiability of LoRA factors (equivalent rescalings of A and B). Consequently, closeness under this penalty need not imply parameter or functional stability.

The remaining theory is largely the standard closed-form behavior of proximal regularization under a linearized, quadratic MSE surrogate. It neither analyzes the actual cross-entropy objective nor establishes that PESO improves future recommendation risk, so claims of data-aware direction-wise adaptation are substantially stronger than the result supports.

The main improvements are often small, especially on Movies & TV and Books, but the paper reports no repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests. It is therefore unclear whether several claimed gains are robust rather than training or decoding variance.

The evaluation protocol is internally inconsistent: the model is said to update over D2 through D5, while headline results are averaged only over D2 through D4 without explaining the exclusion of D5. Per-stage results are absent, and the learning-rate and lambda selection procedures do not clearly state whether only validation data were used.

The stability evidence is not convincing. The explicit forgetting table shows PESO forgetting more than single evolving LoRA on most past blocks; labeling this forgetting 'benign' is post hoc and unsupported. The dormant/new-user results are tiny, single-run differences and use only one dataset.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the reproducibility claim: the advertised code URL is blank, and important details such as LoRA rank and target modules, optimizer, batch size, epochs or stopping criteria, seed protocol, and tokenizer training are missing or unclear.

Some empirical claims contradict the tables: the paper states that all continual methods outperform static pretraining, although many cumulative-LoRA variants perform substantially worse. Comparisons to traditional recommenders also conflate different architectures and evaluation mechanisms, limiting the conclusions that can be drawn.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and practically important problem: efficient continual adaptation of generative LLM recommenders under temporal preference drift.
PESO is simple and computationally attractive, maintaining one evolving adapter with constant storage rather than accumulating adapters over stages.

The empirical study has useful breadth, including three Amazon categories, Yelp, an additional backbone, multiple continual-LoRA baselines, regularizer ablations, and comparisons with traditional recommenders.

The manuscript is generally clear and includes proofs for its local quadratic analysis. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/materials/38e94174977441c783f328d5e48009ef/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited: anchoring current parameters to their previous values is standard proximal regularization, while the main distinguishing choice—softmax-KL over flattened LoRA parameters—is insufficiently motivated.

The parameter-space regularizer is not invariant to LoRA's factorization symmetries: different rescalings, permutations, or rotations of A and B can represent the same BA update but incur different penalties. Softmax also introduces an unpenalized constant-shift direction that can change BA substantially. This weakens the claimed connection between the penalty and preservation of model behavior.

Corollary 4 is mathematically overstated. Softmax-KL equals one-half of the weighted variance only as a second-order local approximation with a remainder term, as correctly stated in Proposition 5; it is not globally equal 'up to an additive constant' as Equation 14 claims.

The theory is largely a generic result for minimizing a quadratic loss plus a quadratic proximal term. It replaces the actual autoregressive cross-entropy with a scalar-logit MSE surrogate and then assigns speculative preference semantics to curvature eigenvectors. It neither specifically justifies softmax-KL nor establishes the claimed behavior for practical LoRA training.

The empirical improvements are often very small—for example, roughly 0–2% over single evolving LoRA on several Books and Movies metrics—and the paper reports neither multiple-run variation nor statistical significance. Consequently, the evidence does not establish that these differences are robust rather than training noise or hyperparameter-selection effects.

The explicit forgetting results conflict with the stability narrative: in Table 12, PESO forgets more than single evolving and cumulative LoRA on every reported past block except one tie. Calling this forgetting 'benign and adaptive' is post hoc because no experiment connects the forgotten examples to genuinely obsolete preferences.

The evaluation protocol is internally inconsistent. The paper defines four incremental blocks D2 through D5 and says models are updated through stage 5, but repeatedly states that results are averaged only over D2 through D4. Elsewhere blocks are indexed D0 through D3. The role of D5 and the exact final evaluation horizon are therefore unclear.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite the reproducibility statement: no seed count, optimizer, batch size, epoch schedule, LoRA rank or target modules are specified, and the promised code URL in the abstract is blank. Candidate-set construction and whether the semantic tokenizer has transductive access to future items also need clarification.

The stability/plasticity subgroup experiment lacks group sample sizes, uncertainty estimates, and controls for differing user-history lengths. New users are not a clean proxy for temporal preference drift, so Table 3 provides weak support for the central mechanistic claim.

Hyperparameters are selected separately for each dataset, but the validation and selection protocol is not fully documented. Given the stated sensitivity to learning rate and the small reported gains, this omission is consequential.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: efficient continual adaptation of generative LLM recommenders under evolving users, items, and preferences.
PESO is simple, computationally inexpensive, and storage-efficient: it maintains one evolving adapter rather than an adapter collection that grows with the number of stages.

The empirical study is broad, covering three Amazon domains, Yelp, two generative-recommendation backbones, numerous cumulative-LoRA variants, recent continual-PEFT methods, traditional recommenders, full fine-tuning, and cumulative retraining.
Results are consistently favorable across the reported datasets and metrics. The dormant-user/new-user breakdown is also a useful attempt to examine stability and plasticity separately.
The paper is generally well organized and provides clear motivation, mathematical derivations, efficiency analysis, and useful ablations over regularizers, learning rates, and proximal strength.
weaknesses: The evidence is not yet reliable enough for acceptance. Results are reported without repeated runs, uncertainty, or significance tests, despite many improvements being very small—for example, roughly 0–2% over single evolving LoRA on several Books and Movies metrics. It is therefore unclear whether the claimed consistent superiority exceeds training and decoding variance.

The temporal evaluation protocol contains a consequential inconsistency. The data are said to contain four incremental blocks D2–D5 and training is described for stages 2–5, yet the main results are averaged only over D2–D4; D5 statistics are provided but its results are apparently omitted. Appendix sections also switch to D0–D3 indexing. This must be clarified and all incremental stages reported.

The methodological novelty is modest: proximal regularization toward the preceding parameters is a standard continual-learning construction. Applying softmax–KL to flattened LoRA factors is unusual, but its semantics are weakly justified because LoRA factors are not categorical distributions and their coordinates are parameterization-dependent. In particular, equivalent LoRA products BA can result from rescaling or changing the factor basis while receiving very different parameter-space penalties.

The theory is substantially weaker than advertised. The direction-wise interpolation follows from a local quadratic surrogate and applies generically to quadratic proximal objectives; it does not establish behavior for the nonlinear cross-entropy-trained LLM. The claimed data awareness comes from the surrogate loss curvature rather than a data-adaptive mechanism specific to PESO. Moreover, Corollary 4 presents softmax–KL as equal to a weighted variance, although Proposition 3 establishes only a local second-order approximation, and the singular softmax Hessian complicates the generalized-eigen interpretation.

The experiments do not cleanly establish adaptation to preference drift. Large fractions of users and items in each incremental block are new, so gains may reflect cold-start or catalog change rather than evolving preferences of recurring users. The drift classifier can likewise exploit changes in users/items, and its sample construction, uncertainty, and controls are not reported. Counts for the dormant/new-user analysis are also missing.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript lacks essential training details such as LoRA rank and target modules, batch size, optimizer, epochs or stopping criteria, hardware, random seeds, and the precise tokenizer-training setup. The stated code URL is blank in the submitted document, and the per-dataset hyperparameter-selection protocol and tuning fairness across baselines are unclear.
